text: If the mean and the variance of $6,4,a,8,b,12,10,13$ are 9 and 9.25 respectively, then $a+b+ab$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let’s set up two equations from the given mean and variance:

Mean = 9 ⇒ total sum = 8·9 = 72  

Known values sum to 6+4+8+12+10+13 = 53, so  

$a+b=72-53=19.$

Population variance = 9.25 ⇒ 

$\frac{\sum x_{i}^{2}}{8}-9^{2}=9.25⟹\sum x_{i}^{2}=8(81+9.25)=722.$  

Known squares sum to 6²+4²+8²+12²+10²+13² = 529, so  

$a^{2}+b^{2}=722-529=193.$

Now use 

$(a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}⟹19^{2}=193+2ab$  

so  

$361=193+2ab⟹ab=84.$

Finally,  

$a+b+ab=19+84=103.$

Answer: 103 (Option A).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: Let $f:[1,\infty )\to [2,\infty )$ be a differentiable function. If $10\int\limits _{1}^{x}f(\mathrm{t})\mathrm{dt}=5xf(x)-x^{5}-9$ for all $x⩾1$, then the value of $f(3)$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To solve the problem, we start with the given equation:

$10\int\limits _{1}^{x}f(t)dt=5xf(x)-x^{5}-9$

By differentiating both sides with respect to $x$, we have:

$\frac{d}{dx}\left (10\int\limits _{1}^{x}f(t)dt\right )=\frac{d}{dx}(5xf(x)-x^{5}-9)$

The left side simplifies to $10f(x)$. For the right side, using the product rule and the power rule, we get:

$10f(x)=5f(x)+5x\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-5x^{4}$

Rearranging terms, we obtain:

$5f(x)=5x\frac{d}{dx}f(x)-5x^{4}$

Let $y=f(x)$. Thus:

$5y=5x\frac{dy}{dx}-5x^{4}$

Dividing by 5, we have:

$y=x\frac{dy}{dx}-x^{4}$

Rewriting, we get:

$\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{y}{x}=x^{3}$

This is a linear differential equation. The integrating factor (I.F.) is calculated as:

$\text{I.F.}=e^{\int \frac{-1}{x}dx}=e^{-\ln x}=\frac{1}{x}$

Multiplying through by the integrating factor, we have:

$y\cdot \frac{1}{x}=\int x^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{x}dx=\int x^{2}dx=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C$

Thus, we solve for $y$:

$y=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+Cx$

Substituting back, we need to find $C$ using the condition at $x=1$:

Since $\int\limits _{1}^{1}f(t)dt=0$, we substitute:

$10\cdot 0=5\cdot 1\cdot f(1)-1^{5}-9\Rightarrow 0=5f(1)-1-9$

$5f(1)=10\Rightarrow f(1)=2$

Now use $f(1)=2$ in the function:

$2=\frac{1}{3}+C\cdot 1\Rightarrow C=\frac{5}{3}$

The function $f(x)$ is given by:

$f(x)=\frac{x^{4}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}x$

To find $f(3)$:

$f(3)=\frac{3^{4}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}\cdot 3=27+5=32$

Therefore, the value of $f(3)$ is 32.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: Let the point P of the focal chord PQ of the parabola $y^{2}=16x$ be $(1,-4)$. If the focus of the parabola divides the chord $PQ$ in the ratio $m:n,\gcd (m,n)=1$, then $m^{2}+n^{2}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given the parabola $y^{2}=16x$, the point $P$ on the focal chord $PQ$ is $(1,-4)$. We need to determine how the focus divides the chord.

First, express the coordinates for the point $P$ using the parametric form of the parabola. The general parametric equations for the parabola are:

$P(at^{2},2at)\equiv P(4t^{2},8t)\equiv (1,-4)$

The equation $8t=-4$ leads to solving for $t$:

$t=-\frac{1}{2}$

Now, find the coordinates of point $Q$ using the relation $t_{1}\cdot t_{2}=-1$. Therefore:

$Q\left (\frac{a}{t^{2}},\frac{-2a}{t}\right )$

Given the focus $S$ of the parabola is at $(4,0)$, we can find the lengths of $PS$ and $QS$:

The length $PS$ is calculated as:

$PS=a+at^{2}$

And $QS$ is given by:

$QS=a+\frac{a}{t^{2}}=\frac{at^{2}+a}{t^{2}}$

Since the focus divides the chord in a specific ratio $m:n$, and $\gcd (m,n)=1$, we find:

$\frac{PS}{QS}=t^{2}=\frac{1}{4}=\frac{m}{n}$

Thus, the squares of $m$ and $n$ sum up to:

$m^{2}+n^{2}=17$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text:
If the system of equations

$\begin{array}{l} 2x+λy+3z=5 \\ 3x+2y-z=7 \\ 4x+5y+μz=9 \end{array}$

has infinitely many solutions, then $\left (λ^{2}+μ^{2}\right )$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} 2x+λy+3z=5 \\ 3x+2y-z=7 \\ 4x+5y+μz=9 \end{array} \\ \text{For infinite solutions}\Rightarrow \Delta =0=\Delta _{1}=\Delta _{2}=\Delta _{3} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{lllllll} \Delta =\left |\begin{array}{lll} 2 & λ & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 5 & μ \end{array}\right |=0 \\ \Rightarrow -4λ-3λμ+4μ+31=0 \\ \Delta _{1}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} 5 & λ & 3 \\ 7 & 2 & -1 \\ 9 & 5 & μ \end{array}\right |=0\Rightarrow -9λ-7λμ+10μ+76=0 \\ \Delta _{2}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} 2 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & 7 \\ 4 & μ & 9 \end{array}\right |=0\Rightarrow μ+5=0\Rightarrow μ=-5 \\ \Delta _{3}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} 2 & λ & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & 7 \\ 4 & 5 & 9 \end{array}\right |=0\Rightarrow λ+1=0\Rightarrow λ=-1 \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll} \therefore \text{For infinite solution}μ=-5\text{and}λ=-1 \\ \begin{array}{ll} \text{Now}μ^{2}+λ^{2} & =25+1 \\ =26 \end{array} \end{array}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ real matrix such that $A^{2}(A-2I)-4(A-I)=O$, where $I$ and $O$ are the identity and null matrices, respectively. If $A^{5}=αA^{2}+βA+γI$, where $α,β$, and $γ$ are real constants, then $α+β+γ$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} A^{2}(A-2I)-4(A-I)=0 \\ A^{3}-2A^{2}-4A+4I=0 \end{array}$

Multiply by $A$

$\begin{array}{l} A^{4}=2A^{3}+4A^{2}-4A \\ A^{4}=2\left (2A^{2}+4A-4I\right )+4A^{2}-4A \\ A^{4}=8A^{2}+4A-8I \end{array}$

Multiply again by $A$

$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow A^{5}=8A^{3}+4A^{2}-8A \\ \Rightarrow A^{5}=8\left (2A^{2}+4A-4I\right )+4A^{2}-8A \\ \Rightarrow A^{5}=20A^{2}+24A-32I \end{array}$

Comparing with $A^{5}=αA^{2}+βA+γI$

$\begin{array}{l} α=20,β=24,γ=-32 \\ \therefore α+β+γ=20+24-32 \\ =44-32 \\ =12 \end{array}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: If $\lim _{x\to 0}\frac{\cos (2x)+a\cos (4x)-b}{x^{4}}$ is finite, then $(a+b)$ is equal to:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the value of $a+b$ for which the following limit is finite:

$\lim _{x\to 0}\frac{\cos (2x)+a\cos (4x)-b}{x^{4}}$

we start by expanding the cosine functions using their Taylor series:

$\cos (2x)=1-\frac{(2x)^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(2x)^{4}}{4!}-\ldots$

$\cos (4x)=1-\frac{(4x)^{2}}{2!}+\frac{(4x)^{4}}{4!}-\ldots$

Substitute these expansions into the limit expression:

$\lim _{x\to 0}\frac{\left (1-\frac{4x2}{2!}+\frac{(2x)4}{4!}-\ldots \right )+a\left (1-\frac{(4x)2}{2!}+\frac{(4x)4}{4!}-\ldots \right )-b}{x^{4}}$

To ensure that the limit is finite, the linear and quadratic terms must sum to zero. Let's equate the constant terms first:

For the limit to be finite: 

$1+a-b=0$

Equating the coefficients of $x^{2}$:

$-2-8a=0$

Solving the second equation, we have:

$8a=-2a=-1 4$

Substitute $a$ back into the first equation to find $b$:

$1+-1 4-b=0b=1-1 4b=3 4$

Thus, the sum of $a$ and $b$ is:

$a+b=\frac{-1}{4}+\frac{3}{4}=\frac{1}{2}$

Therefore, the correct value of $a+b$ is $\frac{1}{2}$.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: If the image of the point $\mathrm{P}(1,0,3)$ in the line joining the points $\mathrm{A}(4,7,1)$ and $\mathrm{B}(3,5,3)$ is $Q(α,β,γ)$, then $α+β+γ$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
[IMG]


Let $X$ be mid point of $P$ and $Q$, which would be also feet of perpendicular.

Let $X$ divides $A$ and $B$ in $λ:1,λ\neq -1$

$\begin{array}{l} X=\left (\dfrac{3λ+4}{λ+1},\dfrac{5λ+7}{λ+1},\dfrac{3λ+1}{λ+1}\right ) \\ \text{Now}PX⟂AB\Rightarrow PX\leftarrow \cdot AB\leftarrow =0 \\ \begin{array}{l} \left (\dfrac{3λ+4}{λ+1}-1\right )\cdot (4-3)+\left (\dfrac{5λ+7}{λ+1}-0\right )(7-5) \\ +\left (\dfrac{3λ+1}{λ+1}-3\right )\cdot (1-3)=0 \end{array} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \dfrac{2λ+3}{λ+1}+\dfrac{10λ+14}{λ+1}+\dfrac{4}{λ+1}=0 \\ \Rightarrow \dfrac{12λ+21}{λ+1}=0\Rightarrow λ=\dfrac{-7}{4} \\ X=\left (\dfrac{5}{3},\dfrac{7}{3},\dfrac{17}{3}\right ) \end{array} \\ X\text{is mid point of}PQ \\ \begin{array}{l} Q\equiv \left (2\cdot \dfrac{5}{3}-1,2\cdot \dfrac{7}{3}-0,2\cdot \dfrac{17}{3}-3\right )\equiv (α,β,γ) \\ \Rightarrow α+β+γ=\dfrac{2(5+7+17)}{3}-4=\dfrac{58}{3}-4=\dfrac{46}{3} \end{array} \end{array}$

text: If $θ𝜖\left [-\frac{7π}{6},\frac{4π}{3}\right ]$, then the number of solutions of $\sqrt{3}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ-2(\sqrt{3}-1)\mathrm{cosec}θ-4=0$, is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the solutions of the equation $\sqrt{3}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ-2(\sqrt{3}-1)\mathrm{cosec}θ-4=0$, we can begin by solving for $\mathrm{cosec}θ$.

The quadratic equation in terms of $\mathrm{cosec}θ$ is:

$\sqrt{3}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ-2(\sqrt{3}-1)\mathrm{cosec}θ-4=0$

Using the quadratic formula:

$\mathrm{cosec}θ=\frac{2\sqrt{3}-2\pm \sqrt{(2(\sqrt{3}-1))^{2}+4\sqrt{3}\cdot 4}}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Simplifying inside the square root:

$(2(\sqrt{3}-1))^{2}+4\sqrt{3}\cdot 4=4(3+1-2\sqrt{3})+16\sqrt{3}$

This simplifies to:

$4(4-2\sqrt{3})+16\sqrt{3}=16-8\sqrt{3}+16\sqrt{3}=16+8\sqrt{3}$

Therefore, the quadratic gives:

$\mathrm{cosec}θ=\frac{2\sqrt{3}-2\pm 2(\sqrt{3}+1)}{2\sqrt{3}}$

By solving, we find:

$\mathrm{cosec}θ=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{3}},2$

Thus, for each value of the cosecant, $θ$ can take several values that fall within the given interval $[-\frac{7π}{6},\frac{4π}{3}]$:

$θ=\frac{-7π}{6},\frac{-2π}{3},\frac{-π}{3},\frac{π}{6},\frac{5π}{6},\frac{4π}{3}$

These are all the possible solutions for $θ$ within the defined range.
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: Let $A=\{1,2,3,\ldots .,100\}$ and $R$ be a relation on $A$ such that $R=\{(a,b):a=2b+1\}$. Let $(a_{1}$, $a_{2}),(a_{2},a_{3}),(a_{3},a_{4}),\ldots .,(a_{k},a_{k+1})$ be a sequence of $k$ elements of $R$ such that the second entry of an ordered pair is equal to the first entry of the next ordered pair. Then the largest integer k , for which such a sequence exists, is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$(a,b)\in R$ means $a=2b+1$, that is, $a+1=2(b+1)$. Along the chain, $a_{i}+1=2(a_{i+1}+1)$ for $i=1,2,\ldots ,k$, so

$a_{1}+1=2^{k}(a_{k+1}+1).$

Since $a_{k+1}\geq 1$ and $a_{1}\leq 100$,

$2^{k+1}\leq 2^{k}(a_{k+1}+1)=a_{1}+1\leq 101\Rightarrow 2^{k+1}\leq 101\Rightarrow k+1\leq 6\Rightarrow k\leq 5.$

$k=5$ is attained with $a_{6}=1$: the pairs $(63,31),(31,15),(15,7),(7,3),(3,1)$ all lie in R, since $63=2\times 31+1$, $31=2\times 15+1$, $15=2\times 7+1$, $7=2\times 3+1$ and $3=2\times 1+1$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

solution.body:
$x+|x|=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} 2x, & x\geq 0 \\ 0, & x<0 \end{array} \right.$

$\Rightarrow \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+|x|}}$, domain is $x>0$, as $2x\neq 0$

Similarly,

$\begin{array}{lllll} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3x+10-x^{2}}}\text{is defined when}3x+10-x^{2}>0 \\ \begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow  & x^{2}-3x-10<0 \\ \quad (x-5)(x+2)<0 \\ \Rightarrow  & x\in (-2,5) \\ \Rightarrow  & \text{Domain will be}(0,\infty )\cap (-2,5)=(0,5) \\ \Rightarrow  & (1+a)^{2}+b^{2}=1+25=26 \end{array} \end{array}$

text: The line $\mathrm{L}_{1}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{\mathrm{a}}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$ and the line $\mathrm{L}_{2}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{\mathrm{b}}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$. The shortest distance between the lines $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The line $L_{1}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{\mathrm{a}}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$. The line $L_{2}$ is parallel to the vector $\vec{\mathrm{b}}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$.

Equations of the Lines:

Equation of $L_{1}$: 

$𝐫=7\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+2\hat{k}+λ(-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k})$

Equation of $L_{2}$: 

$𝐫=5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}+μ(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k})$

Shortest Distance Between $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$:

The formula for the shortest distance between two skew lines is given by:

$\text{Distance}=\left |\frac{\left (⃗{a}_{2}-⃗{a}_{1}\right )\cdot \left (⃗{b}_{1}\times ⃗{b}_{2}\right )}{\right |⃗{b}_{1}\times ⃗{b}_{2}\left |}\right |$

Calculations:

Vector between the points:

$⃗{a}_{2}-⃗{a}_{1}=(5\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k})-(7\hat{i}+6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$

Cross product of direction vectors:

$⃗{b}_{1}=-3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+4\hat{k},⃗{b}_{2}=2\hat{i}+\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$

$⃗{b}_{1}\times ⃗{b}_{2}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ -3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{array}\right |=2\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-7\hat{k}$

Magnitude of the cross product:

$\left |⃗{b}_{1}\times ⃗{b}_{2}\right |=\sqrt{2^{2}+17^{2}+(-7)^{2}}=\sqrt{342}$

Dot product:

$\left (⃗{a}_{2}-⃗{a}_{1}\right )\cdot \left (⃗{b}_{1}\times ⃗{b}_{2}\right )=(-2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+2\hat{k})\cdot (2\hat{i}+17\hat{j}-7\hat{k})$

$=(-2)(2)+(-3)(17)+(2)(-7)=-4-51-14=-69$

Shortest Distance:

$\text{Distance}=\left |\frac{-69}{\sqrt{342}}\right |=\frac{23}{\sqrt{38}}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: Let $(a,b)$ be the point of intersection of the curve $x^{2}=2y$ and the straight line $y-2x-6=0$ in the second quadrant. Then the integral $\mathrm{I}=\int\limits _{\mathrm{a}}^{\mathrm{b}}\frac{9x^{2}}{1+5^{x}}\mathrm{d}x$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} x^{2}=2y\text{and}y-2x-6=0 \\ \dfrac{x^{2}}{2}-2x-6=0 \\ x^{2}-4x-12=0 \\ x^{2}-6x+2x-12=0 \\ x(x-6)+2(x-6)=0 \\ (x-6)(x+2)=0 \end{array}$

Point of intersection are $(6,18)$ and $(-2,2)$

$(-2,2)$ is in second quadrant

$\begin{array}{l} a=-2,b=2 \\ I=\int\limits _{-2}^{2}\dfrac{9x^{2}}{1+5^{x}}dx\text{..... (i)} \end{array}$

$I=\int\limits _{-2}^{2}\frac{9x^{2}}{1+5^{-x}}dx\text{..... (ii)}$

$\begin{array}{l} \text{Adding (i) and (ii)} \\ \begin{array}{l} 2I=\int\limits _{-2}^{2}9x^{2}dx \\ I=9\int\limits _{0}^{2}x^{2}dx \\ I=9\left (\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\right )_{0}^{2}\Rightarrow I=24 \end{array} \end{array}$

text: If the length of the minor axis of an ellipse is equal to one fourth of the distance between the foci, then the eccentricity of the ellipse is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The length of the minor axis is equal to one-fourth of the distance between the foci. Mathematically, this can be expressed as:

$2b=\frac{1}{4}(2ae)$

This simplifies to:

$b=\frac{ae}{4}$

Given that the relationship between $b$, $a$, and $e$ is:

$\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}=1-e^{2}$

Substitute $b=\frac{ae}{4}$ into the equation:

$\left (\frac{ae}{4}\right )^{2}=a^{2}\cdot \left (1-e^{2}\right )$

Expanding and simplifying gives:

$\frac{a^{2}e^{2}}{16}=a^{2}(1-e^{2})$

Divide both sides by $a^{2}$:

$\frac{e^{2}}{16}=1-e^{2}$

Rearrange and solve for $e^{2}$:

$\frac{e^{2}}{16}+e^{2}=1$

$\frac{17e^{2}}{16}=1$

Solve for $e$:

$e^{2}=\frac{16}{17}$

$e=\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}$

Thus, the eccentricity of the ellipse is:

$\frac{4}{\sqrt{17}}$

text: $4\int\limits _{0}^{1}\left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3+x^{2}}+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}\right )dx-3\log _{e}(\sqrt{3})$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Rationalising, $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3+x^{2}}+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3+x^{2}}-\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}{2}$, so

$I=4\int\limits _{0}^{1}\dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{3+x^{2}}+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}=2\int\limits _{0}^{1}\left (\sqrt{x^{2}+3}-\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\right )dx$

Using $\int \sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}dx=\dfrac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}+\dfrac{a^{2}}{2}\log _{e}\left (x+\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}\right )$:

$\int\limits _{0}^{1}\sqrt{x^{2}+3}dx=1+\dfrac{3}{2}\log _{e}3-\dfrac{3}{2}\log _{e}\sqrt{3}=1+\dfrac{3}{2}\log _{e}\sqrt{3}$

$\int\limits _{0}^{1}\sqrt{x^{2}+1}dx=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\log _{e}\left (1+\sqrt{2}\right )$

$I=2+3\log _{e}\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}-\log _{e}\left (1+\sqrt{2}\right )$

$I-3\log _{e}\sqrt{3}=2-\sqrt{2}-\log _{e}\left (1+\sqrt{2}\right )$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text: Let $\vec{\mathrm{a}}=2\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+\hat{k},\mathrm{b}\leftarrow =3\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ and a vector $\vec{\mathrm{c}}$ be such that $(⃗{a}-⃗{c})\times ⃗{b}=-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}$ and $⃗{a}\cdot ⃗{c}=3$. If $⃗{b}\times ⃗{c}=⃗{d}$, then $|⃗{a}\cdot ⃗{d}|$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To solve the problem, we start with the given equation:

$(⃗{a}-⃗{c})\times ⃗{b}=-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}.$

Expanding this, we have:

$⃗{a}\times ⃗{b}-⃗{c}\times ⃗{b}=-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}.$

Since $-⃗{c}\times ⃗{b}=⃗{b}\times ⃗{c}=⃗{d}$, substituting this into the equation, we get:

$⃗{a}\times ⃗{b}+⃗{d}=-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}.$

Now, we take the dot product of both sides with $⃗{a}$:

$⃗{a}\cdot (⃗{a}\times ⃗{b})+⃗{a}\cdot ⃗{d}=⃗{a}\cdot (-18\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+12\hat{k}).$

Since the dot product $⃗{a}\cdot (⃗{a}\times ⃗{b})$ is zero (the dot product of any vector with the cross product of itself with another vector is zero), we have:

$⃗{a}\cdot ⃗{d}=-36+9+12=-15.$

Thus, the magnitude of $⃗{a}\cdot ⃗{d}$ is:

$|⃗{a}\cdot ⃗{d}|=15.$

text:
Given three identical bags each containing 10 balls, whose colours are as follows :

$\begin{array}{llll}  & \text{Red} & \text{Blue} & \text{Green} \\ \text{Bag I} & 3 & 2 & 5 \\ \text{Bag II} & 4 & 3 & 3 \\ \text{Bag III} & 5 & 1 & 4 \end{array}$

A person chooses a bag at random and takes out a ball. If the ball is Red, the probability that it is from bag I is p and if the ball is Green, the probability that it is from bag III is $q$, then the value of $\left (\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}\right )$ is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Probability that a Red ball comes from Bag I ($p$):

$p(B_{1}/R)=\frac{p(B_{1})\cdot p(R/B_{1})}{p(R)}$

Substituting the values,

$p(B_{1}/R)=\frac{\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{3}{10}}{\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{4}{10}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{5}{10}}$

Simplify to find $p$:

$=\frac{\frac{1}{10}}{\frac{1}{3}(1.2)}=\frac{1}{4}$

So, $p=\frac{1}{4}$.

Probability that a Green ball comes from Bag III ($q$):

$p(B_{3}/G)=\frac{p(B_{3})\cdot p(G/B_{3})}{p(G)}$

Substitute the values,

$p(B_{3}/G)=\frac{\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{4}{10}}{\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{5}{10}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}\times \frac{4}{10}}$

Simplify to find $q$:

$=\frac{\frac{2}{15}}{\frac{1}{3}\times 1.2}=\frac{1}{3}$

So, $q=\frac{1}{3}$.

Calculation of $\left (\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}\right )$:

$\frac{1}{p}=4,\frac{1}{q}=3$

Therefore,

$\left (\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}\right )=4+3=7$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift

text: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}+2y\sec ^{2}x=2\sec ^{2}x+3\tan x\cdot \sec ^{2}x$ such that $y(0)=\frac{5}{4}$. Then $12\left (y\left (\frac{π}{4}\right )-\mathrm{e}^{-2}\right )$ is equal $to_____________________$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{dy}{dx}+2y\sec ^{2}x=2\sec ^{2}x+3\tan x\sec ^{2}x \\ \text{I.F.}=e^{\int 2\sec ^{2}xdx} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} \text{I.F.}=e^{2\tan x} \\ y\cdot e^{2\tan x}=\int e^{2\tan x}(2+3\tan x)\sec ^{2}xdx \end{array} \\ \text{Put}\tan x=u \\ \begin{array}{l} \sec ^{2}xdx=du \\ y\cdot e^{2u}=\int e^{2u}(2+3u)du \\ y\cdot e^{2u}\Rightarrow \dfrac{2e^{2u}}{2}+3\int e^{2u}\cdot udu \\ y\cdot e^{2u}=e^{2u}+3\left [\dfrac{ue^{2u}}{2}-\int \dfrac{e^{2u}}{2}\right ] \\ ye^{2u}=e^{2u}+3\left [\dfrac{ue^{2u}}{2}-\dfrac{e^{2u}}{4}\right ]+C \\ ye^{2\tan x}=e^{2\tan x}+3\left [\dfrac{\tan xe^{2\tan x}}{2}-\dfrac{e^{2\tan x}}{4}\right ]+C \end{array} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} y(0)=\dfrac{5}{4} \\ \dfrac{5}{4}=1-\dfrac{3}{4}+C \\ \dfrac{5}{4}-\dfrac{1}{4}=C \\ 1=C \\ y=1+3\left (\dfrac{\tan x}{2}-\dfrac{1}{4}\right )+1\cdot e^{-2\tan x} \\ y\left (\dfrac{π}{4}\right )=1+3\left (\dfrac{1}{2}-\dfrac{1}{4}\right )+\dfrac{1}{e^{2}} \\ y\left (\dfrac{π}{4}\right )=\dfrac{7}{4}+\dfrac{1}{e^{2}} \\ 12\left (y\left (\dfrac{π}{4}\right )-\dfrac{1}{e^{2}}\right )=12\left (\dfrac{7}{4}+\dfrac{1}{e^{2}}-\dfrac{1}{e^{2}}\right )=21 \end{array}$

text: Let $\mathrm{A}(4,-2),\mathrm{B}(1,1)$ and $\mathrm{C}(9,-3)$ be the vertices of a triangle ABC . Then the maximum area of the parallelogram AFDE, formed with vertices D, E and F on the sides BC, CA and $AB$ of the triangle $ABC$ respectively, $is___________$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 2nd April Evening Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The maximum area of such a parallelogram $AFDE$, with one vertex fixed at $A$ and the other three points lying on the sides of triangle $ABC$, is half the area of triangle $ABC$.


[IMG]


Using the determinant formula for area of triangle with vertices $A(x_{1},y_{1}),B(x_{2},y_{2}),C(x_{3},y_{3})$ :

Area $△ABC$

$=\frac{1}{2}|x_{1}(y_{2}-y_{3})+x_{2}(y_{3}-y_{1})+x_{3}(y_{1}-y_{2})|$

Substitute the coordinates:

$\begin{array}{l} =\dfrac{1}{2}|4(1-(-3))+1((-3)-(-2))+9((-2)-1)| \\ =\dfrac{1}{2}|4(4)+1(-1)+9(-3)| \\ =\dfrac{1}{2}|16-1-27|=\dfrac{1}{2}|-12|=\dfrac{12}{2}=6 \end{array}$

Maximum area of parallelogram $AFDE$ $=\frac{1}{2}\times$ area of triangle $=\frac{1}{2}\times 6=3$
